Little did Jack Stone know that Baron von Hess had already forced the captive geologist to begin excavation, intent on securing the rare crystals for his own nefarious ends. Nor was Jack aware that his own benefactor was presumed lost in a jungle expedition, and that Pip was on his trail to deliver a vital message. The skiff’s oversized cooling fins did not hinder the Desert Runner’s progress, whether she was on the salt flats, the shifting dunes, or in a rock-strewn canyon, as she was designed to handle much greater stress. Pip was so thrilled with their successful navigation of the Razorback Ridge that he grabbed his harmonica and played a jaunty tune as the sand-skiff glided along. The recent sandstorm had left a wide path of destruction, scouring the desert floor down to the bedrock and piling loose sand into mountainous drifts.

“Had the Runner been caught in that blow,” said the Professor, “we would have been stripped to the frame by now.”

“A good thing we found shelter in that canyon, then,” answered Jack. “Now to find the Whispering Chasm.”

“It’s at the foot of the Obsidian Peaks, is it not?”

“Yes,” answered the Professor. “Why would the Baron take Dr. Aris there?”

“To keep his operation hidden from the prospector patrols in the main valley.”

“You believe he has a purpose for such secrecy?”

“It is my firm belief that he has Dr. Aris on his mobile fortress, and does not want the patrols to discover it. In a remote, forsaken place like the chasm, where his rig is now, he can force the man to work, and the world will be none the wiser. Do you not see the logic?”

“That is exactly what I suspected, Professor.”

At that moment, a massive, horned sand-crawler scuttled into view from behind a cluster of sun-bleached rocks. The creature waved its fearsome pincers at the vehicle, and with a hiss, it began to charge.

“There’s a dangerous specimen!” ejaculated the Professor.

“And a fast one at that.”

“I think we could disable it.”

“With the static rifle?”

“Yes; if I can get a clear shot.”

“Do it.”

“You take the helm.”

Jack grasped the control yoke, increased the turbine’s whine, and the Professor took the rifle and stepped onto the outer platform. The crawler was moving with surprising speed, its many legs churning up a cloud of dust, and the sand-skiff raced to intercept it. A high pitched hum came from the turbines and a loud scraping from under the wide composite treads. Fast as the crawler was, it was no match for the Desert Runner, which steadily closed the distance.

“The beast is making for that narrow ravine,” said Jack. “Can you cut it off before it gets there?”

“Yes. That will bring us closer to the chasm.”

“Then do it. I need to get in range.”

The crawler was aiming for the safety of the ravine; but, for some cause, it was running in a wide, arcing path. Jack, instead of following in the creature’s wake, now steered the skiff on a direct intersecting course. They had closed half the distance when the Professor lifted the static rifle and fired. A bolt of blue energy struck the crawler, which seized up and toppled onto its side.

“Excellent! You’ve stopped it!” cried Jack. “Steer toward it, Professor.”

The Professor was about to obey the command when the ground suddenly gave a great shudder and cracked open under the skiff. Then it collapsed. Down sank the Desert Runner into the sudden abyss, followed by a landslide of sand and rock. There was a cavern beneath the thin crust of the desert floor. She had fallen into it. The cavern was ancient and deep, so that when the skiff broke through she fell a full twenty feet before crashing onto a bed of soft, damp sand. The ceiling over a wide area had given way all around the Desert Runner. It was to avoid this weak ground that the crawler had been running in a circle was now quite plain.

A chunk of falling rock struck the Professor a glancing blow and knocked him over the rail into the darkness. Scarcely had he vanished from sight when more debris rained down, and he was gone. Pushed down a steep, sandy slope, he tumbled for some distance. When he came to a stop, he was at the edge of an underground pool. It was so dark he could not tell water from rock. For an instant the Professor was so dazed that he thought all was lost; then he gathered his wits, and realizing his peril, he began to crawl forward. It was good fortune that he chose the correct direction, for he soon saw the faint glow of the Runner’s emergency lights. Had he gone the other way he certainly would have been lost in the labyrinthine dark. Grasping a fallen rock, he pulled himself up until he could see the skiff, and then made his way toward it.

No one knew what had happened to him until he climbed back aboard, where he found Jack and Pip assessing the damage.

“Good heavens! What is all this?” asked Jack.

“Knocked overboard by a falling rock.”

“Blimey, Professor, why didn’t you shout?” asked Pip.

“I hardly had time to think.”

“You’d best check for injuries and have a drink from the flask,” advised Jack; “or, by Jove! you will be in no shape to continue.”

The Professor chuckled and went to the medical kit. When he returned with a small bandage on his forehead, he showed no other ill effects from his shocking fall. He found his companions working on a plan to escape the pit into which the crawler had tricked them.

“The only way is straight up,” said the Professor. “Engage the vertical lift turbines.”

This strategy was enacted. The skiff rose slowly on columns of roaring air and landed on solid ground again. As soon as the Desert Runner was safely beside the chasm’s edge, the Professor took a small sample of the crawler’s armored shell. Then they continued their journey toward the mountains. Deep ravines and sheer cliffs now defined the landscape, and a vigilant watch was kept for the Baron’s fortress. As they advanced the terrain grew even more treacherous. They navigated winding canyons, crossed fields of razor-sharp obsidian, and skirted the edges of vast, bottomless pits. The entire region had a grim and forbidding aspect, utterly devoid of life, yet marked by the signs of immense industrial labor. Mountains of tailings and discarded machinery littered the landscape.

League after league was covered. At last the Professor made a new calculation, and consulting his charts, he said to his companions in the cockpit:

“We must be very near to the Whispering Chasm now.”

“Well, it’s no whisper I’ve heard, only the wind,” said Pip.

“Nor have I,” said Jack. “But our distance and heading confirm we are close,” insisted the Professor.

Pip was about to make a reply when there came a sharp cry from Jack, at the forward viewport.

“There’s a structure ahead!”

Everyone was on their feet in an instant. They rushed to the armored glass. Off to the left they saw the machine. As soon as the Professor saw it he cried:

“It is the Baron’s Land-Fortress!”

The colossal machine, its treads dug into the rock, was parked at the very mouth of a great chasm in a basin of black rock, below a mesa upon which the Desert Runner had just come to a halt.

CHAPTER V.

INTO THE VIPER’S NEST.

The sight of Baron von Hess’s fortress so near sent a charge of anticipation through the crew of the Runner. Not a single guard was visible upon the fortress, and the Professor at once caused the sand-skiff to reverse until it was hidden from view.

“Well,” said Jack Stone, “there is the machine we have been seeking. What do you propose to do, Professor?”

“First I must confirm that Dr. Aris is aboard.”

“How will you manage that?”

“I shall go down alone and scout the perimeter.”

“That is an extremely risky proposition.”

“Indeed, sir; but a necessary one.”

“Very well, we will maintain a close watch from here, and if it appears you require aid, Pip and I will be ready to come to your assistance.”

“That is agreeable.”

And with that, the Professor armed himself with a pair of gas-powered pistols and a climbing axe, and leaving the Runner, he moved silently into the night. At some distance from the skiff, he found a narrow game trail that led down from the mesa to the chasm floor. The area around the fortress was brightly lit, but the surrounding cliffs were cast in deep shadow, except for a path that led from the chasm to the fortress’s main hatch. The Professor made his way down to the basin floor.

The Professor made his way down to the basin floor. He crept along the shadowed edge of the chasm, his gaze fixed upon the colossal machine. Its dark metal hull, scarred and pitted from countless journeys across the wastes, seemed to absorb the light. The only sounds were the whisper of the wind and the distant hum of powerful generators deep within the fortress’s belly.

He needed to get closer, to learn if his old friend and colleague, Dr. Aris, was truly a prisoner within that metal beast. The main hatch was a great ramp, now drawn up and sealed tight, an impassable barrier of reinforced steel. The Professor scanned the hull for any other point of entry, but the Baron’s design was brutally efficient, offering no obvious weakness.

As he watched, a small panel slid open near the base of the fortress, and two figures emerged. They were guards, clad in the Baron’s gray and black uniform, carrying heavy-looking pulse rifles. They began a slow, circuitous patrol around the machine’s perimeter.

“A fine night to be freezing our whiskers off, eh, Gunther?” said the first guard, his voice carrying clearly in the still air.

“Quiet, Klaus. You know the Baron does not like chatter on duty,” the second guard grumbled.

“The Baron isn’t out here. He’s snug in his command center, likely counting his money and polishing his monocle. While we’re out here guarding a pile of junk.”

“This ‘pile of junk’ is the most powerful mobile fortress on the continent,” Gunther retorted, though without much conviction. “And within it, the key to the Baron’s ultimate victory.”

“The Aetheric Resonator, you mean?” Klaus scoffed. “A madman’s dream. All it does is make the lights flicker and give the prisoner, Aris, a headache. I heard him screaming again today.”

The Professor’s heart went cold. It was true. Aris was inside.

“They say the final calibration is almost complete,” Gunther said, lowering his voice slightly. “Tomorrow, at dawn, they move the device to the geyser fields. The Baron plans to tap the planet’s own energy. He says it will make him a king.”

“It will make us all irradiated corpses, more like,” Klaus muttered. “I wish that Professor he’s so afraid of would just show up and blow this whole monstrosity to smithereens.”

The Professor flattened himself behind a large outcropping of obsidian as the guards rounded the far side of the fortress. He had the information he needed, and it was worse than he had feared. Not only was Aris a prisoner, but he was being forced to complete a device of unimaginable power, and the deadline was mere hours away.

He had to get back to the Runner. He began to retrace his steps, keeping to the deepest shadows, when a brilliant beam of light shot out from a turret high on the fortress, sweeping across the chasm floor. The Professor froze, pressing himself into a crevice in the rock. The light was blindingly intense. It passed over his position once, twice. He held his breath.

Suddenly, a new sound joined the hum of the generators; a rhythmic clanking and whirring. From another hatch, a mechanical monstrosity emerged. It was a Clockwork Sentry, a man-sized automaton of brass and steel, its single red optic glowing balefully as it scanned the terrain. It moved with an unnatural, jerky gait, its metal feet scraping on the rock.

The sentry’s head swiveled, its optic beam tracing the path of the larger searchlight. The Professor knew that if that red light fell upon him, it would mean the end. The automaton was less than thirty yards away and closing. He had to move.

Waiting for the main searchlight to swing away, he darted from his hiding place, making a break for the game trail. It was a desperate gamble. A loose stone tumbled under his foot, clattering down the rocks.

Instantly, the Clockwork Sentry stopped. Its head snapped in his direction, the red optic flaring. A high-pitched siren wailed from its torso.

There was no time for stealth. The Professor scrambled up the trail, his climbing axe in his hand. He could hear the automaton’s metallic footfalls hastening behind him, faster than he would have thought possible. A searing bolt of energy sizzled past his head, striking the cliff face and showering him with hot stone fragments.

He reached the top of the mesa, gasping for breath, and sprinted for the dark shape of the Desert Runner.

“Professor, what is it?” cried Jack, seeing him burst from the darkness.

“Trouble! They’ve seen me!” he panted.

He clambered aboard just as the Clockwork Sentry appeared at the mesa’s edge. Pip, without a word, threw the main drive lever forward. The Runner’s turbines screamed to life, and the skiff shot forward, leaving the automaton shrinking in the distance. Another energy bolt went wide, splashing harmlessly against the night sky.

Once they were a safe distance away, concealed in another canyon, the Professor recounted what he had learned.

“So Aris is alive!” Jack exclaimed. “But in the gravest peril.”

“And this Aetheric Resonator sounds like a world-ending piece of work,” added Pip. “What are we to do, Professor? We can’t take that fortress head-on.”

“No,” the Professor agreed, his breathing now steady. “We cannot fight it with brute force. We must use our wits. The guards mentioned they are moving the device at dawn. That is our opportunity.”

“How so?” asked Jack. “They’ll be on high alert.”

“Precisely. They will be focused on the transport. They will expect an attack on the convoy, not on the fortress itself. We must strike before they leave.”

“A frontal assault is still suicide,” Jack insisted.

“I do not propose a frontal assault,” the Professor said, a gleam in his eye. “I propose a diversion. Pip, you are an excellent shot with the sonic cannon, are you not?”

“The best there is, Professor!” Pip said proudly.

“Very good. On the far side of that mesa, there is a large, unstable rock formation, a veritable spire of sandstone. I want you to stay with the Runner. At my signal, you will fire the cannon and bring that spire down. The noise and destruction should draw the majority of the Baron’s forces, including that patrol, to the west side of the fortress.”

“And while they’re lookin’ that way?” Pip asked.

“While they are distracted,” the Professor continued, turning to Jack, “you and I will enter the fortress from the east. The guards’ chatter gave me another clue. They complained of the Resonator making the lights flicker. That implies a tremendous power draw, and a tremendous power draw requires cooling and ventilation.”

“You found a vent?” Jack asked.

“I believe so. A large grate, high up on the eastern face, away from the main entrance. It is our only way in. We will rescue Dr. Aris and sabotage the Resonator before the Baron can move it.”

“It’s a long shot, Professor,” Jack said, his jaw set. “But it’s the only one we have.”

“Then let us prepare,” the Professor declared. “The fate of our friend, and perhaps much more, rests upon our success this night.”

They made their way back toward the fortress, this time approaching from the east. The Desert Runner came to a halt in a deep ravine, perfectly hidden from view but with a clear line of sight to the sandstone spire. The Professor and Jack, armed and equipped with climbing gear, disembarked.

“Give us thirty minutes to get into position,” the Professor told Pip over the radio. “When you see three green flares, unleash your fury. And be ready for a quick extraction.”

“Aye, Professor. I’ll be waiting. Good luck to you both.”

The two men began the perilous ascent of the fortress’s hull. The metal was cold and smooth, offering few handholds. They moved slowly, methodically, using magnetized grapples and their own strength to inch their way upward. The wind howled around them, threatening to tear them from their precarious perch. Below, the chasm floor was a pit of absolute blackness.

After a tense twenty minutes, they reached the ventilation grate. It was just as the Professor had surmised; a massive louvered panel, twenty feet wide, humming with the force of the air being drawn through it.

“Now for the tricky part,” Jack muttered.

The Professor produced a small device from his pack, a vibro-cutter. He applied it to the bolts holding the grate in place. The tool whined, the sound terrifyingly loud in the relative quiet. They both froze, listening for any sign of alarm, but there was none. One by one, the bolts loosened and fell away. With a final heave, they pried a section of the grate open, revealing a dark, cavernous shaft.

The Professor took out his flare gun and fired three quick bursts of green light into the night sky. Almost immediately, a low hum echoed from the direction of the Desert Runner, followed by a deafening boom that shook the very hull of the fortress. A moment later, they heard a tremendous crash and the rumble of thousands of tons of rock giving way.

“Pip’s done his part,” Jack said, peering through the grate. “The diversion has begun.”

Alarms began to shriek from within the fortress. They could hear the sounds of running feet and shouted commands from far below.

“Now is our chance,” said the Professor. “Follow me.”

He swung himself into the ventilation shaft, and Jack followed close behind. They were plunged into a world of roaring air and grinding machinery. The shaft was a maze of fans and conduits, slick with oil and condensation. They crawled on their hands and knees, the noise a constant, deafening roar.

They crawled for what felt like an eternity, following the schematics the Professor had memorized from a stolen blueprint of a similar, older model of the Baron’s fortresses. Finally, they came to another grate, this one in the floor of the shaft.

The Professor peered through. They were directly above the fortress’s main engineering deck. It was a vast chamber filled with pistons, gears, and dynamos, all working in a furious, chaotic symphony of industrial power. In the center of the room, cordoned off by crackling energy fences, was a massive, spherical device, glowing with a sickening purple light. It was the Aetheric Resonator. And chained to a console beside it was a haggard, white-haired man in a tattered lab coat.

“Aris!” the Professor whispered.

There were two guards posted at the console, their attention now focused on a large screen displaying the chaos outside. This was their moment.

Jack used the vibro-cutter to silently remove the grate. They dropped to the deck below, landing with soft thuds behind a bank of machinery. The guards, distracted by the alarms and the scene on the monitor, noticed nothing. The Professor and Jack moved like shadows, coming up behind the two men. A pair of swift, precise blows, and the guards slumped to the floor, unconscious.

The Professor rushed to his friend’s side. “Aris! It’s me, William!”

Dr. Aris looked up, his eyes wide with disbelief. “William? Is it really you? I thought I was hallucinating again.”

“We’re getting you out of here,” Jack said, using a laser torch to cut through the chains.

“You don’t understand!” Aris cried, his voice hoarse. “You have to get away! The Resonator, it’s unstable! My last calculation was a bluff to buy time, but the Baron didn’t believe me. He ordered the final power-up sequence to begin. When the main geyser fires at dawn, the feedback loop will be catastrophic! It won’t just power his fortress; it will shatter the entire tectonic plate!”

Just then, a klaxon of a different pitch began to sound. Red lights flashed throughout the chamber. On the screen, the external view was replaced by a familiar, chilling face, complete with a monocle and a sneer.

“Professor,” the voice of Baron von Hess boomed from the speakers, cool and menacing. “How kind of you to drop in. Did you really think I would be fooled by such a childish diversion? Your friend, the rock-thrower, has been neutralized. As for you, you have merely saved me the trouble of bringing my little experiment to you. You have arrived just in time for the grand finale.”

On the screen, they could see the Desert Runner, caught in a tractor beam, being pulled inexorably toward the fortress.

“Pip!” Jack yelled.

“There is no escape,” the Baron’s voice echoed. “The Resonator is at ninety percent. In ten minutes, the entire region will become my personal, inexhaustible power source, and you will have the honor of being the first to be atomized by its glory.”

“We have to stop the overload!” Aris gasped, now free of his chains.

“How?” asked the Professor.

“The primary coolant system! It’s our only chance. If we can flood the reaction chamber, it might cause a cascade failure, but it’s better than letting the reaction complete!”

“Where is it?” Jack demanded.

“Through that door! The main coolant control valve!” Aris pointed to a heavy blast door across the chamber.

As if on cue, the door slid open, and Baron von Hess himself stepped through, flanked by two more Clockwork Sentries. He was a tall, imposing man in a pristine military uniform, and in his hand, he held an ornate, gold-plated energy pistol.

“I think not,” the Baron said with a thin smile. “The performance has reached its climax. I must insist you stay and watch.”

CHAPTER VI. THE DEVIL’S CAULDRON.

“Jack, get Aris to the controls!” the Professor shouted. “I will deal with the Baron!”

Jack didn’t hesitate. He grabbed the frail Dr. Aris and half-dragged, half-carried him toward the coolant valve station, while the Professor advanced on the Baron.

“So, the great Professor means to challenge me personally?” the Baron sneered. “You, a man of books and theories, against a man of action and will?”

“Your will is bent on nothing but destruction, Hess!” the Professor shot back. “It ends now!”

The Clockwork Sentries raised their weapons, but the Baron held up a hand. “No. This pleasure is mine alone.”

He fired his pistol. The Professor dove behind a massive piston, the energy bolt exploding against the metal. He returned fire with his own gas-powered pistol. The projectile struck the Baron’s uniform but bounced off an unseen personal energy shield.

“Your toys are quaint, Professor,” the Baron mocked, advancing slowly.

Meanwhile, Jack and Aris reached the coolant control station. It was locked. “The override code!” Aris yelled over the din. “He’s locked it out!”

Jack paid him no mind. He raised his foot and delivered a powerful kick to the control panel’s casing. It bent, but held. He kicked it again, and again, his heavy boots denting the metal. With a final, mighty blow, the lock sparked, fizzled, and broke.

“It’s open!” Jack cried, yanking the twisted panel away.

“Turn the wheel! All the way to the left!” Aris instructed, his fingers flying over a secondary keypad, bypassing safety protocols.

The Baron saw what was happening. His sneer vanished, replaced by a mask of fury. “Insolent fools!” he roared, turning his pistol toward Jack.

But the Professor was ready. He leaped from behind the piston, his climbing axe in hand. He didn’t aim for the Baron, but for a thick, high-pressure steam pipe running overhead. With a desperate swing, he struck the pipe. The axe bit deep. A jet of superheated steam erupted from the gash, directly into the Baron’s path.

The Baron cried out, more in anger than pain, as the steam fogged his shield and his vision. It was the opening the Professor needed. He charged, not at the Baron, but at the Clockwork Sentries. When he arose his head was under a piece of floating debris. It held him under the glowing fluid so he could not breathe. For an instant Jack was so bewildered that he felt sure he was going to dissolve; then he pulled his faculties together, and realizing his position, he dove under and swam under the surface. “I scarcely had time to even breathe.”

As soon as Jack was able to climb out into the corridor, the Professor went around the problem by remotely activating a small maintenance drone to bring him a fresh change of clothes and a med-pack. Mighty atriums rose here and there, vast holographic displays were crossed, executive shuttles were traversed, and they had to skirt the bases of huge decorative sculptures and towering hydroponic gardens. Everything presented a wild and picturesque appearance, perfectly sterile as far as common workers were concerned, and yet teeming with security bots and surveillance drones. How these machines were all powered in this isolated section was a mystery; but it was clear that they drew a very significant energy load, as was evidenced by the thick, glowing power conduits.

“Neither have I,” said the doctor. “But the distance traveled warrants the belief that we are near it,” persisted Jack.

The Professor was just about to reply when there came a yell from Pip, who was monitoring the ship’s enhanced sensors from the cockpit.

The Baron’s ship, stripped of its stealth cladding and showing its ostentatious gold trim, was moored to a private docking bay in a great basin below an observation deck upon which Jack had just come to a pause.

“First ascertain if the kidnapped scientist is aboard of her.”

“How will you go about it?”

“I’m going down there to ask them.”

“That’s a suicidal piece of business.”

“Very true, sir; but I am not afraid to venture.”

“Well, we will keep a sharp watch upon your movements from up here, and if we see that you need our assistance, the Desert Runner itself will be ready to blast its way down to your aid.”

“That suits me.”

The guards on the ramp were facing away from him, supervising the loading of several large, mysterious-looking crates. Jack made his way down the corridor.

“With pleasure, me boy!” the Professor cackled, his fingers dancing over his weapons console.

They were setting up a heavy repeating blaster on a tripod, preparing to lay down a field of overwhelming fire.

“No you don’t,” Jack muttered to himself.

He took aim with his stun pistol and fired three quick shots. The blue rings of energy flew across the bay. One struck the repeating blaster, causing it to spark and short out. The other two hit the guards operating it, who stiffened and fell to the deck, unconscious.

Jack did not flinch. He dove behind a large cargo container for cover, his mind already formulating a plan to get past the squad and onto the Baron’s ship.
